name: Kurukh
confidence_why: The word-class reading rests only on Hahn's 1911 missionary grammar, whose claim that two-syllable words always carry initial accent is contradicted by Lakra 2019, the one modern first-hand description, which finds accent on the first or second syllable of disyllables according to vowel length; neither is a phonological study, and the fuller descriptions by Pinnow 1964, Gordon 1976 and Kobayashi & Tirkey 2017 have not been checked. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Hahn 1911 1911.

catalog_quote: § 13. In words which have only two syllables the accent is always on the first : puddā, short; bāckā, word. In words of three syllables the verbs have generally the accent on the second syllable, tisignā to open, kirta'anā, to return; except in those which end in ba'anā, e.g., guchāba'anā, which take the accent on the third syllable. There are rare instances of verbs of three syllables having the accent on the first : nisigna, to dress a wound; nedegnā, to fall off, are examples. Adverbs, however, as a rule take the accent on the first syllable, even though they are of three or four syllables except when they are compounds, like nelbenjā, the day after to-morrow, mundbhāre, ahead, etc.; in these the accent is on the first syllable of the second word, that is the second syllable of the compound word. new_statements.quote: When a word which has more than one syllable is uttered then one of the syllables gets more prominence than the other. In some disyllabic words the first syllable gets more prominence whereas in other words the second syllable gets more prominence. [...] In disyllabic words below, the accent falls on the second syllable. [...] The first syllable is more prominent than the second syllable as in the first syllable the vowel is prolonged and is accented than the second syllable. [...] I the above trisyllabic words, the stress have fallen in first, second and third syllables. [...] But this can be observed in most of words the stress has fallen on the second syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: matches; sec. '2.6. STRESS AND INTONATION' at lines 1019-1095 (thesis pp. 83-84). Every sentence in the compiler bracketed quote is present verbatim, including the typos 'I the above trisyllabic words, the stress have fallen'. Read the section: 13 examples; in all 11 with a long vowel the accent sits on the (leftmost) long-vowel syllable (e.g. ʈʌʈ-xˈɑ:, en-ɖˈe:r, mˈe:-nəɪ, ˈʧɑ:-ɖe, pɒ-ˈxɑ:-ri:, bɪɖ-put-ˈtɑ:, nɪŋ-ˈɡi:-jɒ); the two without a long vowel split (kʌt-ˈtʰən second, xˈʌd-dɑr first, the latter noted by the author as accented without a prolonged vowel); author says accent is fixed per word but 'there are times where the accent depends upon the function of the words in a sentence' and…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (prominence) falls on the syllable with the long vowel: second syllable in disyllables like ʈʌʈ-xˈɑ: 'mango', en-ɖˈe:r 'what'; first syllable in mˈe:-nəɪ 'listen', ˈʧɑ:-ɖe 'evening'; in trisyllables it lands on first, second or third syllable but 'in most of words.. on the second syllable' (pɒ-ˈxɑ:-ri: 'pond', er-ˈʧe:r-num 'sweat'). The author calls the accent fixed per word but says it can also depend on the word's function in the sentence. Not a clean rule; length attraction is the only conditioning factor stated.
new_statements.exceptions: xˈʌd-dɑr 'children' is first-syllable accented without a long vowel; 'There are times where the accent depends upon the function of the words in a sentence.'
new_statements.identity_note: Works 0 and 1 (Gordon 1973, 1976) describe Dhangar-Kurux, the Kurux spoken by the Dhangar people of Morang and Sunsari Districts, Kosi Zone, southeastern Nepal (chief consultant from Kusaha, Morang District), heavily influenced by Indo-Aryan. Lakra 2019 describes Kurukh in and around Ranchi, Jharkhand. Work 2 is a multi-language word-list volume covering eight ISO codes including kru.

sources.quote: 'In some disyllabic words the first syllable gets more prominence whereas in other words the second syllable gets more prominence.' Second-syllable accent: got-tˈa: (collective), tat-xˈa: 'mango', en-dˈe:r 'what', kat-ˈtʰən 'tale' -- 'for the above words the accent for the syllable is fixed'. First-syllable accent: mˈe:-nəi 'listen', ˈʧa:-de 'evening', xˈʌd-dar 'children' -- 'the first syllable is more prominent ... as in the first syllable the vowel is prolonged'. Trisyllables (ʧiʧ-ˈja:r-a: 'shout', er-ˈʧe:r-num 'sweat', po-ˈxa:-ri: 'pond', bid-put-ˈta: 'entire day', niŋ-ˈgi:-jo 'your mother'

sources.note: Word-list volume; the Dhangar-Kudux phonological note names length, nasalization and gemination only and says nothing about stress, matching the compilers finding for Gordon's clause paper in Part II of the same series (suprasegmentals = length and gemination only). Neither supports nor contradicts Hahn 1911 or Lakra 2019. The McAlpine 2000 re-edition (text, a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/pitch/tone over all 544 pp.) has accent/tone statements only for the Tibeto-Burman languages of Hale's Nepal volume (Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Kham, etc.), none for Dhangar-Kudux.
